name: Founder content
description: Voice, post formats and the approve-then-post workflow.

cards.subject: Voice
says: is the consistent personality that makes a writer's posts recognisable
stays constant across topics and formats
cards.use: want posts to sound like the same person every time
not: changes completely with each platform

cards.subject: Tone
says: shifts to suit the situation while the underlying voice stays the same
is warmer in a condolence reply than in a product announcement
cards.use: adjust how you sound for a sensitive reply
not: is fixed for the life of a personal brand

cards.subject: A voice guide
says: records how a writer sounds, with examples and words to avoid
lets a second person or a tool draft in the writer's voice
cards.use: need someone else to draft in your voice
not: removes the need to review drafts

cards.subject: Plain language
says: prefers short, common words over jargon
lets a busy reader grasp the point on a first read
cards.use: write for readers outside your specialism
not: signals that the author lacks expertise

cards.subject: First person
says: speaks as I from lived experience rather than as an institution
makes a claim attributable to one named person
cards.use: want to share something you actually did
not: is only suitable for company pages

cards.subject: A specific example
says: replaces an abstract claim with a concrete case
gives the reader something they can check
cards.use: notice a sentence could have been written by anyone
not: makes a post longer without making it clearer

cards.subject: Banned phrases
says: is a list of cliches and filler the writer never uses
catches the generic wording that drafting tools tend to produce
cards.use: want to keep stock phrases out of drafts
not: is a list of topics the writer must avoid

cards.subject: Point of view
says: states a position a reader could disagree with
gives a post something to say beyond summarising the news
cards.use: want a post to say more than the news already says
not: is the same as being controversial for attention

cards.subject: The byline-blind test
says: hides the author's name and asks readers whether the post sounds like the author
shows voice drift that the author cannot see in their own drafts
cards.use: suspect edited drafts have moved away from the author's style
not: measures how many people liked the post

cards.subject: Voice drift
says: is the slow shift away from the established voice as drafts pass through many hands
goes unnoticed because each single edit looks small
cards.use: see posts that each look fine but feel less and less like the author
not: happens only when the author changes topic

cards.subject: A sponsored-content disclosure
says: tells readers a post was paid for or incentivised
must be clear and visible rather than buried
cards.use: post something you were paid to say
not: is optional when the post is positive

cards.subject: An affiliate link disclosure
says: tells readers the author may earn a commission if they buy through the link
appears where the reader sees it before clicking
cards.use: share a link that pays you when someone buys
not: is satisfied by a note in the profile alone

cards.subject: A gifted-product disclosure
says: applies even when no money changed hands
covers free items, trips and early access
cards.use: received a free item and want to mention it
not: is only needed when the gift is worth a large sum

cards.subject: An own-company disclosure
says: states that you own or work for the business you are praising
stops a promotion from reading as independent praise
cards.use: recommend your own product or employer
not: is unnecessary when the product is good

cards.subject: A material connection
says: is any relationship that could affect how readers weigh a recommendation
includes payment, free products, family ties and employment
cards.use: wonder whether a relationship with a company needs disclosing
not: exists only when money has been paid

cards.subject: An AI-assistance disclosure
says: tells readers when a tool generated or heavily shaped the content
matters most where readers would assume a person wrote or experienced it
cards.use: publish text or images that a model produced
not: is needed only for images, never for text

cards.subject: A synthetic-media label
says: marks an image, voice or video as generated or altered
guards against readers taking a realistic fake for a recording of something real
cards.use: publish a realistic generated video of a person
not: is only needed when the content is political

cards.subject: A confidentiality check
says: confirms a post reveals no client, employer or unreleased detail without permission
happens before the draft goes for approval
cards.use: want to share a story from client work
not: is satisfied by changing the client's logo to a generic one

cards.subject: A testimonial permission
says: records consent before a customer is quoted by name
covers use of their words and their logo
cards.use: want to quote a customer's praise
not: is implied once a customer says thank you

cards.subject: The reasonable-reader test
says: asks whether an ordinary reader would understand the relationship at a glance
fails a disclosure hidden among a block of hashtags
cards.use: judge whether a disclosure is clear enough
not: is passed by any disclosure that exists somewhere in the post

cards.subject: A text-only post
says: relies on the words alone with no attachment
suits a single clear idea or short story
cards.use: have one idea that needs no visual
not: performs worse than any other format

cards.subject: A hook
says: is the opening line that makes a reader continue
does its work before the rest of the text is collapsed
cards.use: need the first line to earn the reader's attention
not: is a closing summary of the post

cards.subject: A carousel
says: splits an idea across swipeable slides
suits step-by-step explanations and frameworks
cards.use: explain a process in steps readers can swipe through
not: is the best format for breaking news

cards.subject: A short video
says: lets the audience see and hear the author
suits demonstrations and personal stories
cards.use: want people to see how you work or hear your voice
not: needs no planning because it is informal

cards.subject: A poll
says: asks the audience to choose from a few options
gives a one-tap response but shallow engagement
cards.use: want a quick signal on audience preference
not: produces detailed qualitative feedback

cards.subject: A call to action
says: tells the reader the one next step you want
offers a single step so the reader is not asked to choose
cards.use: want the reader to do one specific thing after reading
not: is required at the end of every post

cards.subject: A recap post
says: summarises an event or week for people who missed it
turns notes taken at the time into something reusable
cards.use: attended an event others could not
not: must cover everything that was said

cards.subject: A story post
says: follows a situation, a turn and a lesson
builds trust by showing a real decision
cards.use: have a lived experience that taught you something
not: works best as a list of tips with no event

cards.subject: A myth-busting post
says: names a common belief and presents evidence against it
needs a real counter-example to avoid being contrarian for its own sake
cards.use: hear readers repeat a belief you have seen fail
not: is stronger when it attacks a named person

cards.subject: A behind-the-scenes post
says: shows how work is actually done, mistakes included
humanises the author without announcing a result
cards.use: want to show the process rather than the outcome
not: is only for finished, polished work

cards.subject: A long-form article
says: develops an argument at length with room for evidence
suits reference material that readers return to
cards.use: have an argument that cannot be made in a short post
not: is the quickest way to start a conversation

cards.subject: A value-adding comment
says: adds a fact, example or question beyond agreement
gives the author and other readers something new
cards.use: want your comment to be worth reading
not: simply agrees with the post

cards.subject: A generic comment
says: says little more than 'great post'
could be pasted under any post unchanged
cards.use: see a reply that fits every post equally
not: builds a relationship with the author as well as a thoughtful one

cards.subject: Commenting before posting
says: has the author join other people's conversations before publishing
builds familiarity with the audience where they already are
cards.use: are new to a topic and have an audience to find
not: replaces the need to publish original posts

cards.subject: Replying to comments on your own post
says: answers readers who commented on your post
keeps the conversation going and shows readers they were heard
cards.use: someone has commented on your post
not: is a distraction from the real work of posting

cards.subject: Tagging
says: notifies another person that a post mentions them
is used only when the person would want to see the post
cards.use: mention someone whose work you are crediting
not: is a good way to get strangers to notice a sales post

cards.subject: Moderation
says: removes spam and abuse from the comments on your own post
is applied by a stated rule rather than dislike of disagreement
cards.use: find spam or abuse in your comments
not: means deleting every comment that disagrees

cards.subject: Engagement bait
says: asks for likes or comments for their own sake
trades reader goodwill for short-term numbers
cards.use: see a post that says 'comment YES if you agree'
not: is a reliable way to attract the right readers

cards.subject: Disagreeing in public
says: states the point of difference politely and addresses the argument, not the person
moves to a private message if the exchange turns personal
cards.use: disagree with another author's claim in their comments
not: is best done by quoting them in a post that names them

cards.subject: Responding to a hostile comment
says: answers once, calmly and with facts, or does not answer at all
avoids a back-and-forth the audience has to watch
cards.use: get a rude comment from someone in public
not: needs a reply every time to show you are not afraid

cards.subject: Commenting on a competitor's post
says: adds value without pitching your own offer under their post
treats the comment section as the other author's space
cards.use: want to join a discussion on a rival's post
not: is the best place to link your own service

cards.subject: A cold DM
says: is the first message to someone who has not engaged with you
is judged on whether it is relevant to the recipient
cards.use: message someone you have never spoken to
not: is expected to be answered quickly

cards.subject: A warm DM
says: follows an existing interaction such as a comment or reply
can refer back to the comment or reply that prompted it
cards.use: someone has just replied to your post
not: is the same as a cold DM with a friendlier greeting

cards.subject: A connection request note
says: says in a line why you want to connect
is short and carries no sales pitch
cards.use: send a connection request to someone new
not: should include your whole offer

cards.subject: An unsolicited pitch
says: asks for a sale or meeting in the first message
puts the sender's goal ahead of the recipient's
cards.use: are tempted to sell in your first message
not: tends to get replies because it is direct

cards.subject: The one-question message
says: asks a single easy question
makes replying cheap for the recipient
cards.use: want a stranger to find it easy to answer
not: lists several questions to save the recipient time

cards.subject: A follow-up DM
says: adds something new rather than repeating 'just checking in'
is sent once or twice and then stops
cards.use: have had no reply to your first message
not: is sent weekly until the person answers

cards.subject: Opting out
says: is honoured immediately when someone says stop
ends all further outreach to that person
cards.use: someone asks you not to message them again
not: is treated as a no for now and revisited next quarter

cards.subject: A DM template
says: gives a starting structure that is personalised before sending
becomes spam when sent unchanged to many people
cards.use: write similar messages regularly
not: can be sent unchanged to save time

cards.subject: Moving a conversation off-platform
says: happens only after the other person shows interest
is offered as a choice rather than pushed in the first reply
cards.use: want to continue a conversation by email or a call
not: is requested in the first message

cards.subject: Sensitive information in a DM
says: is not requested over message, such as passwords or payment details
is a warning sign of a scam when a stranger asks for it
cards.use: someone asks you for account details by message
not: is acceptable if the sender looks professional

cards.subject: A lead
says: is a person or company that has shown possible interest
has not yet agreed to buy
cards.use: need a word for someone who has shown early interest
not: is any follower of the account

cards.subject: Lead capture
says: records who showed interest and where they came from
stores contact details with the person's awareness
cards.use: want to note an enquiry before it is forgotten
not: means collecting contact details without telling people

cards.subject: A lead log
says: is a simple record of each enquiry, its status and the next step
stops enquiries from being forgotten
cards.use: enquiries are arriving by comment, DM and email
not: is only needed once volume is high

cards.subject: A lead source
says: names the post, comment, DM or referral that brought the lead
shows which content produces enquiries
cards.use: want to know which content brings enquiries
not: is the lead's job title

cards.subject: Lead qualification
says: checks need, budget, authority and timing before time is invested
separates good-fit enquiries from curiosity
cards.use: receive an enquiry and must decide how much time to give it
not: rejects any lead that has not bought before

cards.subject: A response-time target
says: sets how soon every enquiry gets a first reply
is tracked so slow replies become visible
cards.use: enquiries are going unanswered for days
not: promises a finished proposal within the same day

cards.subject: Consent for follow-up
says: is needed before someone is added to a mailing list
is separate from a person simply replying to a message
cards.use: want to add an enquirer to a newsletter
not: is given whenever a person sends a DM

cards.subject: BANT
says: tests budget, authority, need and timeline
is one checklist for qualifying a lead
cards.use: want a quick checklist for a new enquiry
not: scores how many followers the lead has

cards.subject: A handoff
says: passes a lead to the person who will sell or deliver
carries the history so the lead is not asked the same things again
cards.use: get an enquiry that belongs with another person on the team
not: transfers only the lead's name

cards.subject: A nurture sequence
says: sends useful content to a lead who is not ready yet
stops when the person opts out or buys
cards.use: hear from a good-fit lead that it is not the right time
not: keeps sending offers until the lead buys

cards.subject: Disqualifying politely
says: declines a poor-fit enquiry with a reason and a pointer elsewhere
keeps the relationship intact for later
cards.use: receive an enquiry clearly outside what you can deliver
not: is done by ignoring the message

cards.subject: An approval workflow
says: moves a draft through defined steps before it is published
names who can approve
cards.use: want drafts to follow the same route to publication
not: lets anyone publish as soon as they finish writing

cards.subject: The approve-then-post rule
says: means nothing goes live until the owner has approved the final text
applies to drafts written by a person or generated by a tool
cards.use: have a ready draft that someone asks to publish
not: lets a trusted drafter publish first and have it reviewed later

cards.subject: An approval checklist
says: lists checks such as facts, links, disclosure and tone
is the same for every post
cards.use: want reviewers to check the same things each time
not: is rewritten for each post

cards.subject: A single approving owner
says: is the one named person whose approval releases a post
prevents a post being approved by everyone and so by no one
cards.use: have a post whose reviewers each assume another signed off
not: means other reviewers cannot comment

cards.subject: A fact check
says: verifies every claim, number and quote against a source
happens before approval, not after publication
cards.use: have a draft that contains a statistic
not: is satisfied by the drafter's memory of the figure

cards.subject: A publishing log
says: records what was posted, when and who approved it
supports correcting or removing a post later
cards.use: need to find out who approved an old post
not: lists only the posts that performed well

cards.subject: An AI-generated draft
says: gets the same review as one written by a person
is never published straight from the tool
cards.use: have a post whose text a tool produced
not: can skip fact checks because the tool is confident

cards.subject: A scheduled post
says: is approved first and published later at a set time
is rechecked if news changes before it goes out
cards.use: queue posts in advance
not: is approved at the moment it publishes

cards.subject: A version-locked approval
says: applies to the exact text that was reviewed
is void if the text changes afterwards
cards.use: see an approved draft edited at the last minute
not: carries over to any later edit

cards.subject: A sensitivity review
says: checks whether a post could harm someone or look tone-deaf given current events
is stronger when run by someone who did not write the post
cards.use: worry that a scheduled post may land badly after a news event
not: is the same as a spelling and grammar check

cards.subject: A public correction
says: is added openly when a published post contains an error
keeps trust better than silent editing
cards.use: you find an error in a post that is already live
not: is done by deleting the post and saying nothing

cards.subject: A content calendar
says: lists what will be posted and when
helps a writer plan ahead instead of improvising
cards.use: want to see upcoming posts in one place
not: fixes every post so it cannot change

cards.subject: A posting cadence
says: is the realistic rhythm of posts the author can sustain
matters less than being able to keep it up
cards.use: decide how often to publish
not: should be set as high as the platform allows

cards.subject: A content pillar
says: is a recurring theme the author wants to be known for
gives each post a place in a larger story
cards.use: want your posts to add up to a recognisable subject
not: is a single high-performing post

cards.subject: A topic backlog
says: is a list of ideas kept ready to be scheduled
is fed by questions from comments and DMs
cards.use: keep running out of things to write about
not: is the list of posts already published

cards.subject: A review slot
says: is time set aside to compare the plan with results
feeds what goes into the next calendar
cards.use: want results to shape the next month's plan
not: happens only after a post has failed

cards.subject: Batching
says: writes several posts in one sitting
reduces the cost of switching between tasks
cards.use: find that writing one post a day takes more time than it should
not: means publishing several posts at the same moment

cards.subject: A buffer of drafts
says: is a stock of approved posts ready to go
protects the cadence when the author is busy
cards.use: travel or a deadline will take the author away
not: is a list of posts the author may write someday

cards.subject: An evergreen post
says: stays useful long after it is published
can be reshared later
cards.use: write something that will still be true next year
not: depends on a current news story

cards.subject: A timely post
says: responds to news or an event while it is current
loses value if it waits in the queue
cards.use: need to react to an industry event that has just happened
not: can be scheduled months in advance

cards.subject: Calendar slack
says: leaves open slots for unplanned posts
lets the author respond to events without breaking the plan
cards.use: find every slot in the month already full
not: is wasted time that should be filled

cards.subject: Repurposing
says: turns one idea into several formats
keeps the core message while changing the form
cards.use: want more value from an idea you have already developed
not: means reposting the identical text everywhere

cards.subject: A pull quote
says: extracts one striking line from a longer piece
stands alone as a short post
cards.use: want a short post from a long article
not: rewrites the whole article as one sentence

cards.subject: A comment-to-post idea
says: turns a good question from the comments into a new post
credits the person who asked if they are named
cards.use: see a reader ask a question many others may share
not: copies the commenter's words without credit

cards.subject: A pillar piece
says: is a substantial work that smaller posts are cut from
keeps the smaller posts consistent with one argument
cards.use: plan a series of posts from one major piece
not: is a post chosen because it received the most likes

cards.subject: A text-to-carousel conversion
says: maps each point of a written post onto one slide
trims the wording to fit a slide
cards.use: want to turn a list post into a visual
not: pastes the whole post onto the first slide

cards.subject: A transcript-to-post workflow
says: turns the transcript of a recording into written posts
needs editing so spoken filler does not carry over
cards.use: recorded a talk or call that others would find useful
not: publishes the raw transcript as the post

cards.subject: Adapting to a platform
says: changes length, format and opening to suit where the post appears
avoids pasting the same text everywhere
cards.use: want one idea on several platforms
not: means keeping the same wording on each

cards.subject: An FAQ post
says: answers a question that keeps arriving in DMs
reuses the answer as public content
cards.use: keep giving the same answer to the same question
not: is written without checking what readers ask

cards.subject: Recycling an evergreen post
says: republishes an old post with a fresh angle or update
is done after checking that the facts still hold
cards.use: have an old post that is still relevant
not: reposts it unchanged every week

cards.subject: A repurposing cap
says: limits how many times one idea is reshaped
guards against the audience meeting the same point repeatedly
cards.use: followers have started to notice the same message again and again
not: is a limit on how many platforms to use

cards.subject: A target audience
says: is the specific group of people the content is written for
is narrower than everyone online
cards.use: decide who a post is for
not: is every person who might see the post

cards.subject: Consistency
says: is showing up regularly with a recognisable theme
builds familiarity over time
cards.use: want readers to recognise your work
not: means posting identical content

cards.subject: An audience persona
says: describes a typical reader's role, problems and goals
is built from real conversations rather than guesses
cards.use: want a concrete picture of the reader
not: is a list of demographic guesses

cards.subject: Buying followers
says: inflates the count with accounts that never read posts
damages credibility and engagement rates
cards.use: are tempted to raise a follower count quickly
not: is a shortcut to a real audience

cards.subject: Niche focus
says: narrows the topic so the right readers recognise the author
trades breadth for a clearer reputation
cards.use: want to be known for something specific
not: grows an audience by covering as many topics as possible

cards.subject: A collaboration post
says: features or co-creates with another author
exposes the work to that person's audience
cards.use: want to reach readers who already follow someone relevant
not: works best with someone who shares your audience exactly

cards.subject: A newsletter
says: gives the author a direct channel to subscribers who opted in
does not depend on a platform's feed
cards.use: want to reach readers without relying on a feed
not: reaches everyone who follows you on a platform

cards.subject: Social proof
says: shows others' endorsement such as testimonials and shares
persuades more when it is specific and verifiable
cards.use: want visitors to believe a claim about your work
not: is more persuasive when it is anonymous and general

cards.subject: Owned audience
says: is the contact list the author controls, such as email subscribers
survives changes to a platform's rules
cards.use: worry that a platform could change reach or close the account
not: is the follower count on a platform

cards.subject: Rented audience
says: is followers on a platform whose rules and reach the platform controls
can disappear with a policy change
cards.use: depend entirely on one platform for contact with readers
not: belongs to the author like an email list

cards.subject: A community
says: is a space where members talk to each other, not only to the author
grows through shared interest and moderated norms
cards.use: want readers to connect with each other as well as with you
not: is the same as a large follower count

cards.subject: A vanity metric
says: looks impressive but does not show progress toward a goal
includes raw follower and like counts
cards.use: want to avoid measuring only what looks good
not: is the best predictor of enquiries

cards.subject: An impression
says: counts each time a post is shown
is not the same as a person reading it
cards.use: see how many times a post was displayed
not: counts the unique people who saw it

cards.subject: Reach
says: counts the unique people who saw a post
is lower than impressions when people see the post more than once
cards.use: want to know how many different people saw a post
not: counts each display of the post

cards.subject: Engagement rate
says: divides interactions by the people or views who could have interacted
lets posts of different reach be compared
cards.use: want to compare a small post with a large one fairly
not: is the total number of likes

cards.subject: A baseline
says: is the starting level against which change is judged
must be recorded before an experiment begins
cards.use: plan to test a change in your posts
not: is set after the results are in

cards.subject: A leading indicator
says: changes early and predicts later results
includes replies from target readers
cards.use: want an early sign that content is working
not: confirms results only after the work is done

cards.subject: A lagging indicator
says: moves after the fact, such as closed work or revenue
confirms results but is slow to guide changes
cards.use: want proof that content led to business results
not: changes first and predicts what follows

cards.subject: Qualitative feedback
says: comes from replies and DMs that explain why a post mattered
reveals reasons numbers cannot
cards.use: want to know why a post resonated
not: is a count of reactions

cards.subject: A conversion rate
says: is the share of people who take the next step
is judged against the step the post asked for
cards.use: want to know how many readers acted on a call to action
not: is the number of people who saw the post

cards.subject: Attribution
says: links an enquiry or sale back to the content that influenced it
is imperfect, so asking 'how did you hear of me?' complements it
cards.use: receive an enquiry and want to know what prompted it
not: is exact when tracked by clicks alone

cards.subject: An A/B comparison of posts
says: changes one element, such as the hook, and compares results
is unreliable when many things differ between the posts
cards.use: want to learn which opening works better
not: compares two posts on different topics and days

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: warns that a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
explains why chasing likes can degrade content
cards.use: notice posts being written to raise one number
not: says a metric becomes more reliable once it is a target

cards.subject: Authenticity
says: means the posts match what the author actually thinks and did
is damaged by claims the author cannot back up
cards.use: want readers to trust that you mean what you post
not: means sharing every detail of your life

cards.subject: A fabricated anecdote
says: invents an experience that did not happen
is dishonest even when the lesson is sound
cards.use: are tempted to improve a story with details that did not happen
not: is acceptable if it makes the point clearer

cards.subject: Crediting a source
says: names where an idea or figure came from
stops borrowed work being passed off as original
cards.use: share an idea that came from someone else
not: is needed only for direct quotations

cards.subject: An overclaim
says: states a result more strongly than the evidence supports
is avoided by saying what you saw and what you do not know
cards.use: want to describe a result from one case
not: is harmless when the post is meant to inspire

cards.subject: Admitting a failure
says: shares a real mistake and what changed afterwards
builds trust more than a stream of successes
cards.use: made a mistake from which others could learn
not: damages credibility regardless of how it is told

cards.subject: A humblebrag
says: wraps self-praise in a complaint or modest wording
tends to read as insincere
cards.use: are tempted to announce an achievement as a hardship
not: is a modest way to share good news

cards.subject: Personal boundaries
says: decide in advance what the author will not share
protect family, clients and employer
cards.use: are unsure whether a personal detail belongs in a post
not: are drawn after seeing which details attract engagement

cards.subject: Opinion versus fact
says: labels a personal view as a view
keeps readers able to tell what is verified
cards.use: are about to state a belief as if it were established
not: is a distinction readers do not notice

cards.subject: A ghostwritten post
says: is drafted by another person for the named author to publish
remains acceptable when the views, experiences and approval are the author's own
cards.use: someone else drafts posts under your name
not: is dishonest whenever someone else holds the pen

cards.subject: A generic AI voice
says: shows in even rhythm, stock openers and abstract claims
is fixed by editing in specifics only the author knows
cards.use: read a draft that is smooth but could be anyone's
not: is a sign that the draft is ready to publish

cards.subject: An engagement pod
says: is a group that agrees to boost each other's posts
distorts the signals that show what really resonates
cards.use: are invited to join a group that likes and comments on each other's posts
not: is an honest way to find your real audience

cards.subject: A crisis response
says: acknowledges the issue, states facts and says what will change
pauses scheduled posts while the issue is handled
cards.use: face a post that has caused real offence and is spreading
not: defends the original post and deletes critical comments

qa.q: What is the difference between voice and tone?
qa.right: Voice is the consistent personality; tone adapts to the situation
wrong: Tone is the consistent personality; voice adapts to the situation
Voice is for written posts and tone for video
They are two words for the same thing
qa.why: Voice stays constant; tone flexes with context.

qa.q: Which opening line is the strongest hook?
qa.right: "I lost a client last month because of one sentence in my proposal."
qa.why: A specific, concrete opening gives a reason to keep reading.

qa.q: What does an impression count?
qa.right: Each time a post is displayed
wrong: The number of unique people who saw it
The number of people who clicked
The number of people who commented
qa.why: Impressions count displays, not people.

qa.q: Why should an affiliate disclosure appear before the link?
qa.right: Readers should know about the commission before they click
wrong: Links work only after a disclosure
It lets the platform rank the post higher
It is needed only for links to your own site
qa.why: Disclosure is meant to be seen at the moment it affects the reader's decision.

qa.q: Which is a value-adding comment under a post about onboarding?
qa.right: "We cut drop-off by writing the first task as a question; has that worked for you?"
wrong: "Nice, check out my course on this."
qa.why: It adds a specific example and a question; the others add nothing or pitch.

qa.q: What is the main risk of an unsolicited pitch in a first DM?
qa.right: It puts the sender's goal ahead of the recipient's, so it is ignored
wrong: It breaks a platform rule in every case
It is read by too many people
It is too short to be read
qa.why: Cold pitches fail on relevance and reciprocity.

qa.q: Which element makes a disclosure fail the reasonable-reader test?
qa.right: It sits in a block of hashtags at the end of the post
wrong: It appears in the first line in plain words
It names the company that paid
It is repeated in the video caption
qa.why: An ordinary reader would not notice it.

qa.q: What does a version-locked approval mean?
qa.right: The approval covers only the exact text that was reviewed
wrong: The post can never be edited again
Any later edit keeps the approval
Approval lasts until the end of the month
qa.why: Changed text needs fresh approval.

qa.q: A content calendar has no gaps. What is the main drawback?
qa.right: The author cannot respond to news without breaking the plan
wrong: Drafts cannot be approved in advance
qa.why: Slack leaves room for reactive posts.

qa.q: Which metric is a leading indicator for a founder who wants consulting enquiries?
qa.right: Replies from people in the target audience
qa.why: It changes early and relates to the goal, unlike revenue (lagging) or counts (vanity).

qa.q: What is the best use of a transcript from a recorded talk?
qa.right: Edit it into several written posts, removing spoken filler
wrong: Publish it unedited as one long post
Delete it once the video is posted
qa.why: Repurposing needs editing for the written form.

qa.q: Why is an email list called an owned audience?
qa.right: The author controls the contact list regardless of a platform's rules
wrong: It has more members than any social platform
qa.why: Platform followers are rented; email subscribers are portable.

qa.q: Which statement about a ghostwritten post is most accurate?
qa.right: It can be honest when the views, experiences and approval are the named author's
wrong: It is acceptable only for company pages
It must be labelled as AI-generated
qa.why: Honesty rests on the author's real stance and sign-off.

qa.q: What does Goodhart's law say?
qa.right: A measure used as a target stops being a good measure
wrong: Every metric should have a target
qa.why: Targets invite gaming.

qa.q: A founder's draft tells a story about a client rescue. Details come from a real project but the client is identifiable. What should happen first?
qa.right: Run a confidentiality check and get permission or anonymise
wrong: Publish it because the story is flattering
Wait to see whether the client complains
qa.why: Client details need permission before approval.

qa.q: A tool generated a post draft and the facts look plausible. What is the right next step?
qa.right: Fact-check every claim, then send it through the normal approval
wrong: Publish it because it looks plausible
Skip approval because the tool did the drafting
Ask the tool to confirm its own facts and publish
qa.why: Tool drafts get the same review as any other.

qa.q: A post has been approved and scheduled. A major news event happens before it goes live. What should you do?
qa.right: Recheck the post and pause it if it could land badly
wrong: Let it publish because it was approved
Edit it and publish without re-approval
qa.why: Approvals are tied to the context they were given in.

qa.q: You discover a wrong figure in a post that is already live. What is the best response?
qa.right: Add a visible correction and note the change
wrong: Delete the post and say nothing
Leave it because most readers have seen it
qa.why: Open corrections keep trust.

qa.q: Someone comments rudely on your post and others are watching. What is the best response?
qa.right: Answer once, calmly and with facts, or let it stand
wrong: Quote their comment in a new post naming them
qa.why: Avoid a public argument.

qa.q: A stranger replies to your post with interest. What is the best DM?
qa.right: Refer to their reply and ask one easy question
wrong: Send a long message describing your services
Ask for a meeting in the first message
Send the same template you used for cold outreach
qa.why: A warm DM builds on shared context.

qa.q: A prospect says 'please stop messaging me'. What do you do?
qa.right: Stop at once and record the opt-out
wrong: Wait a month and ask again
Move them to a mailing list
qa.why: An opt-out is honoured immediately.

qa.q: An enquiry arrives asking for work far outside what you offer. What is the best response?
qa.right: Decline politely with a reason and point to a better fit
wrong: Accept it and work it out later
Quote a high price to put them off
qa.why: Polite disqualification protects the relationship.

qa.q: You received a free product and want to post about it, with no payment. What should the post include?
qa.right: A clear note that the product was given free
wrong: Nothing, because no money changed hands
Only a hashtag in the comments
A note only if the product is expensive
qa.why: Gifts are a material connection.

qa.q: A post you published earlier performed well. You plan to repost it unchanged next week. What is the better approach?
qa.right: Revisit it later with a fresh angle after checking facts
wrong: Delete it and write something entirely new
Copy it to every platform at once
qa.why: Recycling needs a new angle and a fact check.

qa.q: A post gets many likes but no enquiries over three months. What do you conclude?
qa.right: Likes may be a vanity metric; check replies and enquiries against the goal
wrong: The post format is the only problem
Likes always lead to enquiries eventually
qa.why: Align metrics with the goal.

qa.q: A founder notices recent posts read smooth but generic. What should they do first?
qa.right: Edit in specifics only they know and review the voice guide
wrong: Remove all examples to shorten posts
qa.why: Generic voice is fixed by specifics.

qa.q: Two editors keep rewriting the founder's drafts toward their own styles. What would reveal the effect?
qa.right: A byline-blind test with readers
qa.why: It shows whether the voice is still recognisable.

qa.q: A community member invites you into a group where everyone likes each other's posts. What's the concern?
qa.right: It distorts the signals about what really resonates
wrong: You will lose followers at once
qa.why: Pods inflate engagement and mislead the author.

qa.q: A post you scheduled caused real offence and is spreading. What is the right first move?
qa.right: Pause scheduled posts, acknowledge and state the facts
wrong: Defend the post and hide critical replies
Post a joke to change the subject
qa.why: Respond openly and stop the pipeline.

qa.q: An author wants to test whether a shorter hook works better. What is the sound design?
qa.right: Change only the hook between two comparable posts and compare
wrong: Change the topic, format and hook together
Post on different days with different topics
Compare the new post with a post from last year
qa.why: One change at a time.

qa.q: Two reviewers each assume the other approved a post and it goes live unchecked. What process fix helps?
qa.right: Name a single approving owner
qa.why: A single owner closes the gap.

qa.q: A customer says 'thanks, loved it!' in a DM. You want to quote it on your site with their name. What is needed?
qa.right: Their permission to use the words and name
wrong: Nothing, since they wrote it to you
qa.why: Testimonials need consent.

qa.q: A founder wants to be known for one topic but posts on many. What should they use?
qa.right: Content pillars to focus on recurring themes
qa.why: Pillars give a recognisable subject.

qa.q: A reader asks the same question in DMs for the third time. What should you do?
qa.right: Turn the answer into a public FAQ post
wrong: Send a template with no personal touch
qa.why: Repurpose recurring questions.

qa.q: A rival posts about a topic where you could help. What is the best comment?
qa.right: One useful addition with no link to your own offer
wrong: A claim that their advice is wrong
A direct message sent in the comment
qa.why: Add value, not an ad, in their space.

qa.q: Your author voice guide lists words never to use. Which is the best entry?
qa.right: "Game-changer" and other stock praise words
wrong: Any word with more than three syllables
qa.why: Banned phrases remove cliches.

qa.q: A draft says, 'Our approach always doubles results.' It rests on one client. What is the issue?
qa.right: An overclaim from a single case
qa.why: State what you saw and its limits.

qa.q: A founder wants to move a promising DM conversation to a call. When is it appropriate?
qa.right: After the other person has shown interest, offered as a choice
qa.why: Let interest come first.

qa.q: A lead says it is not the right time but fits well. What should you do?
qa.right: Offer useful content and note a follow-up date, with their consent
wrong: Add them to a mailing list without asking
qa.why: A nurture sequence respects consent.

qa.q: Which is the best first-line hook for a post about a mistake?
qa.right: "I published a wrong figure to 5,000 people and here is what I did next."
qa.why: Concrete stakes earn attention.

qa.q: Which checklist item is missing from an approval checklist of facts, links and tone?
qa.right: Disclosure of any commercial or AI-assistance relationship
qa.why: Disclosure is a core pre-approval check.

qa.q: An author wants to understand whether content causes enquiries. Which practice helps most?
qa.right: Record the lead source and ask 'how did you hear of me?'
wrong: Check likes on the last post
qa.why: Attribution comes from sources and asking.

qa.q: A founder wants to know why one post resonated. Where is the best evidence?
qa.right: The replies and DMs that explain what mattered
qa.why: Qualitative feedback gives reasons.

qa.q: Your cadence plan says daily posts, but quality is dropping. What should you do?
qa.right: Reduce to a rhythm you can sustain and keep a buffer
qa.why: Sustainable cadence beats ambitious cadence.

qa.q: A realistic video of a person was generated by a model. What should accompany it?
qa.right: A clear label that it is generated
wrong: A label only if it is political
Only a note in the author's profile
qa.why: Synthetic media is labelled for the viewer.

qa.q: A founder is invited to promote a tool and told to say it is 'their favourite'. They haven't used it. What should they do?
qa.right: Decline or say only what they truly think, with disclosure
wrong: Say it is their favourite with a hashtag disclosure
qa.why: Endorsements must reflect real opinion.

qa.q: You paste the same text unchanged on every platform. What is the weakness?
qa.right: It ignores differences in length, format and opening
wrong: It makes the author look less busy
qa.why: Adapt to the platform.

qa.q: An author wants to build a direct channel not dependent on a platform. Which choice fits?
qa.right: A newsletter with opt-in subscribers
qa.why: An owned channel reduces platform risk.
